claims: Temporary Protected Status (TPS) does not automatically lead to a green card.
TPS holders can adjust status if they meet eligibility requirements like family sponsorship, employment-based sponsorship, or a lawful initial entry.
TPS provides a safe harbor to pursue other immigration avenues such as applying for permanent residence if a visa is available.
An immediate relative is a spouse, parent, or unmarried child under 21 who is a U.S. citizen.
Employment-based green cards involve sponsorship by an employer through Form I-140.
Khalique Law PLLC and USCIS say that generally, for adjustment of status (applying for a green card within the U.S.), you must have initially entered the U.S. legally (with inspection/visa).
A previously popular route to "lawful admission" status was traveling on Advance Parole and re-entering.
The Supreme Court barred this for those who initially entered illegally (Sanchez v. Mayorkas).
Immigrant Legal Defense notes that [the Supreme Court ruling in Sanchez v. Mayorkas] does not apply to those who initially entered with a visa and overstayed.
TPS holders must maintain their TPS status through re-registration.
